sections.heading: The definition, and two common exceptions

blocks.p: A **prime number** is a natural number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. A number greater than 1 that isn't prime is **composite**.

**0 is neither prime nor composite**: the two words are only defined for natural numbers greater than 1. (0 couldn't pass the test anyway: every non-zero number divides 0, so it has far more than two divisors.)
**1 is also neither**: a prime needs exactly two distinct divisors (1 and itself), but 1's only divisor is 1 itself, just one.
**2 is the only even prime.** Every other even number has 2 as a divisor as well as 1 and itself.

**Solution:** It's enough to test divisibility by every prime up to $\sqrt{91} \approx 9.5$ (2, 3, 5, and 7), since any factor larger than the square root would have to pair with one smaller than it, already caught. $91$ is odd (not divisible by 2), its digit sum 10 isn't divisible by 3, it doesn't end in 0 or 5 (not divisible by 5), but $91 = 7 \times 13$, so **91 is composite**, not prime.
Compare 97: $\sqrt{97} \approx 9.8$, and none of 2, 3, 5 or 7 divides it, so **97 is prime**.

sections.heading: Prime factorization and distinct prime factors

blocks.p: The **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** says every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. The primes that appear are its **prime divisors** (or prime factors); counted once each, they are its **distinct** prime factors.
**Example:** factorize 360 and list its distinct prime factors.
**Solution:** Keep dividing by the smallest prime that works: $360 = 2 \times 180 = 2^2 \times 90 = 2^3 \times 45 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$.
Its distinct prime factors are 2, 3 and 5: three of them, even though six primes multiply together to make 360. The exponents also give its number of divisors: $(3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 24$.
A pair of primes exactly 2 apart is called a **twin prime** pair, like $(17, 19)$ or $(29, 31)$. The very first few pairs are $(3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31), (41,43)$.

Two numbers are **co-prime** when their HCF is 1, meaning they share no prime factor. Neither has to be prime itself: $8 = 2^3$ and $15 = 3 \times 5$ are co-prime. Any two different primes are always co-prime.

list: **Calling 1 a prime.** It has only one divisor. The smallest prime is 2.
**Trusting numbers that look prime.** 51 ($3 \times 17$), 57 ($3 \times 19$) and 91 ($7 \times 13$) are the usual traps. Test every prime up to the square root.
**Stopping before the square root.** You need every prime up to $\sqrt{n}$ and no further: 2, 3, 5 and 7 settle 97, but skipping 7 for 91 would miss its factor.
**Mixing up distinct and repeated prime factors.** 360 has three distinct prime factors (2, 3, 5), but six prime factors counted with repetition.
**Thinking co-prime means both numbers are prime.** 8 and 15 are co-prime and neither is prime.

exam.note: Primes and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic open the Real Numbers chapter in Class 10 boards. Prime factorization, number of divisors and co-primes are also staples of quantitative aptitude, including the General Aptitude section every GATE paper carries.
